If I rank y first, I am guaranteed to get y if it's available. If I don't get y, I move down my list.

Given that w > y, I should rank w higher than y.

Now, consider x and z. I value x = $72 and z = $58. I have priority 2 at both. Therefore, I should rank x higher than z.

The question is where to put x and z relative to w and y. Since w and y have priority 1 for me, it makes sense to put them first.

If I rank w > x > y > z, then I get w if available. If not, I get x if available. If not, I get y if available. If not, I get z.
If I rank w > y > x > z, then I get w if available. If not, I get y if available. If not, I get x if available. If not, I get z.

If I rank y > w > x > z, then I get y if available. If not, I get w if available. If not, I get x if available. If not, I get z.

Since w > y, and I can get either w or y for sure, I want to rank w first. So, w > y is better than y > w.

Consider the ranking w > x > y > z vs w > y > x > z.
If I get rejected from w, then I either get x or y. I prefer x to y. So, w > x > y > z is better than w > y > x > z.

Therefore, my optimal ranking is w > x > y > z.
